title: silent submit
scenario: A user submits a slow form. The request starts but the screen gives no reliable signal. The user clicks again and two submissions are created.
outcome: The second action was caused by uncertainty about whether the important state transition had started.

title: unacknowledged command
scenario: A service sends a command to a worker but gets no acknowledgement. The caller retries and the job runs twice.
outcome: Retry without reliable evidence or idempotency created duplicate work.

title: fake spinner
scenario: A UI replaces a missing result with a spinner that stays visible after the operation already failed. Users think work is still progressing.
outcome: Feedback is not automatically useful; misleading feedback can be worse than silence.

title: shared state
scenario: Three unrelated features mutate one global state object. A change for one feature causes a stale value in another feature.
outcome: Independent changes became difficult to reason about because ownership was shared.

title: expert controls
scenario: A power-user tool exposes twenty controls on one screen. Reducing the choices makes experts slower because they intentionally use many controls together.
outcome: Fewer choices are not universally better; the cost of choice depends on user expertise and task structure.

title: valid transaction
scenario: Two database changes are implemented separately for cleanliness, but they must commit together or the system enters an invalid state.
outcome: Separation is useful only when the things can actually change independently.

title: confirmation fatigue
scenario: A product asks for confirmation before every change. Users click through warnings without reading them.
outcome: Friction should not be applied uniformly; repeated low-consequence confirmations become noise.

title: irreversible migration
scenario: A destructive database migration is allowed without an explicit checkpoint or rollback path.
outcome: Higher consequence and lower reversibility justify more friction and stronger safeguards.

title: premature abstraction
scenario: A design system turns two similar screens into one generic component. Later their behaviors diverge and the shared abstraction becomes hard to change.
outcome: Abstraction is not automatically good; it is useful when the underlying behavior is actually shared.

title: helpful duplication
scenario: Two small pieces of code are kept separate because their future changes are independent. A forced shared abstraction would add coordination cost.
outcome: Duplication can be cheaper when independent change is more valuable than reuse.

title: recoverable edit
scenario: A text editor auto-saves every keystroke and provides easy undo. It does not ask for confirmation before edits.
outcome: Low consequence and high reversibility make extra friction unnecessary.

title: idempotent retry
scenario: A service retries a request because the response was delayed, but the operation is idempotent and produces the same final state once or twice.
outcome: Retry is not intrinsically dangerous; its effect depends on state transition semantics.

title: irrelevant progress
scenario: A tiny local rename takes 20 milliseconds. Adding a progress indicator makes the interface feel slower.
outcome: Feedback has a cost and should match the uncertainty and duration users actually need to resolve.

title: independent cache
scenario: Two subsystems have unrelated cache lifecycles but share one invalidation mechanism. A change in one cache causes broad invalidation.
outcome: Shared ownership creates coupling even when the underlying concerns change independently.

title: destructive bulk action
scenario: A bulk delete can remove thousands of records and has no undo. The UI adds an explicit checkpoint and clear consequence information.
outcome: Higher consequence and lower reversibility justify stronger friction.

title: partial failure
scenario: A pipeline hides which stage failed. Operators retry the whole pipeline and unknowingly repeat stages that already succeeded.
outcome: Hidden state makes the next action less reliable and increases accidental repetition.
